title: MA8-09216
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXX XXXXX XXXXX, 32 years old, his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXX, 26 years old, and their daughter XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, five years old, all Mexican citizens, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
XXX XXXXX XXXXX is his minor daughter's designated representative.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX alleged that on XXXXX, 2007, during the municipal elections, she found a number of torn ballots in a plastic bag. She brought the bag home and talked about it with her spouse, XXX, and his brother. They suggested to her that the ballots be taken to the municipal president, XXXXX XXXXX.
Mr. XXXXX became very aggressive when he saw the torn ballots and asked her not to talk about it and threatened to kill them if he had difficulties.

Six weeks later, the claimants decided that it was their duty to report, and they went to see the PRD (party of the democratic revolution) municipal candidate, XXXXX XXXXX, who told them that he could not do much.
On XXXXX, 2007, some AFI officers came to ask her questions, specifying that they came on behalf of Mr. XXXXX.
On XXXXX and on XXXXX, 2008, the claimants participated in a demonstration against electoral fraud.

On XXXXX, 2008, XXXX XXXX and the principal claimant's brother were forced to climb in a bus, and they were beaten. The claimants participated in another demonstration on XXXXX, 2008, and the AFI police officers came to their home and beat the principal claimant, who was alone at home.

The claimants decided then to leave their home and stayed at the male claimant's sister's home, where they remained until XXXXX, 2008, when they saw the AFI officers' van pass by carrying the officers who had attacked them.

Their hosts asked them to leave, and they returned home, but on XXXXX, 2008, the AFI squadron returned to their home and tried to break open their door. The principal claimant exited through the back door and asked for help from people who were playing baseball in a park. These people made the AFI officers flee by yelling at them to leave.
They decided then to leave Mexico and arrived in Montréal on XXXXX, 2008.
The claimants' identity was established in a satisfactory manner through their passport, seized by Immigration Canada.
The claimants' testimony was not clear or precise and contained implausibilities, contradictions and omissions that altered the credibility.

The principal claimant testified that she fears XXXXX XXXXX, former municipal president, and specified that her problems began on XXXXX, 2007, when she took him the damaged ballot boxes that she had found in the building hallways on election day.

She testified that she allegedly brought the ballots home and that it was her husband and her brother-in-law who allegedly advised her to take them to the mayor. When asked why she had not returned them to the election authorities that day, she responded that she had thought about calling someone who had more power and that, when she talked to her brother-in-law, he had told her to take them to the mayor and specified that the mayor is a member of the National Action Party (PAN).

When she was asked how many ballots were in the boxes, she responded that she did not know and then continued by saying that when her brother, spouse and she met the mayor, he threatened them, and six weeks later, they decided to report him.

When asked to explain whether the election results had been announced when they decided to report Mr. XXXXX, she responded that they had and specified that it was a candidate from the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), XXXXX XXXXX, who had been elected.

The principal claimant stated that when she met Mr. XXXXX, he became angry. When asked to explain why in her story she stated that she was disappointed by Mr. XXXXX's reaction, the female claimant responded: [translation] "I was thinking that he could do something". She testified that it was Mr. XXXXX who allegedly told XXXXX XXXXX that she had come to see him. When asked why Mr. XXXXX, who is a PRD member and who won the elections, would allegedly report them to Mr. XXXXX, the female claimant responded: [translation] "I don't know".

In addition, when asked what party she voted for, she responded that she voted for the PRD; when asked to explain why, if she voted for the PRD she reported the torn ballots to the mayor, the outgoing PAN member, the female claimant responded that she had not made the connection between the political party and the fraud, and she specified that she was not politically oriented.

The panel is surprised on the one hand that the fraudsters were negligent enough to leave the torn ballots; it also finds it surprising that the claimants waited six weeks to report the mayor when the elections had finished and he had not won.
However, the most implausible part of this story is that the claimants suggested that there was some complicity between the outgoing mayor, Mr. XXXXX, and Mr. XXXXX, of the opposing party.
The panel is of the opinion that it is implausible that Mr. XXXXX, who is of the PRD, would have reported the people who allegedly informed him of the fraud, of which he was allegedly a victim.

In addition, the claimants alleged that they participated in several demonstrations against election fraud, on XXXXX, 2007, and XXXXX and XX, 2008, organized by some PRD members against the irregularity in the elections.

On XXXXX, 2008, some AFI officers allegedly arrested and beat Messrs. XXX and XXXXX XXXX XXXX and, after the XXXXX, 2008, demonstration, the AFI officers came to their home and allegedly hit the principal claimant and searched the house for the ballots.

When asked to explain who was sending the officers, the principal claimant responded that it was Mr. XXXXX, and when asked why the officers were searching her house looking for the ballots, seeing that she had returned them to him, she responded: [translation] "He thought that there were more".

Although she was not confronted about it, the panel draws a negative inference from the fact that the immigration officer's notes from the interview with the female claimant state: [translation] "on XXXXX, 2008, the officers came again and broke down the door. I went to find help in a baseball park"; however, in her PIF, she alleged that this incident happened on XXXXX and that, on XXXXX, she was at her sister-in-law's home in Mexico City.
The panel finds that this story is not credible; however, even if it were, there would be a reasonable internal flight alternative in this case.

The claimants testified that they went to stay with their sister in Mexico City but believe that they were found there because while they were returning from shopping, and they were in their car, they allegedly saw a van carrying the same AFI officers who had come to their home in XXXXX; they testified that they allegedly lost them and that they returned to their mother's home.

When asked why she thought that these officers were looking for them and whether the fact that they came across them was maybe a coincidence, the principal claimant responded: [translation] "they motioned for us to stop". The panel is of the opinion that it is an adjustment in her testimony and that the claimants did not demonstrate that they had been found in Mexico City by the AFI officers, who never went to their sister's home.

When asked to consider the possibility of settling in Mexico City or in Guadalajara, the principal claimant responded that she does not think it is possible because they will find them with the help of their elector's card.

When asked to explain why Mr. XXXXX would invest time and money to find them, the female claimant responded that the AFI police officers recently went to her mother's home looking for her. Asked to explain why they waited two and a half years to go to her mother's home, she adjusted her testimony and stated that during that period, she would see them pass in front of her home, which was still being watched.
This is a significant omission that undermines the female claimant's credibility.

In addition, when asked to state the location of his brother, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, who allegedly was also beaten and threatened, the male claimant responded that he returned to Mexico and that he lives in XXXXX. When asked whether his brother has problems, he responded that he does not and explained that he has been living there quietly since XXXXX 2010.
The claimants did not discharge their burden of proof and did not show that an IFA does not exist.
For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection".

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim of XXX XXXXX XXXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.
